blocks.text: With תור thor, that is, the turtledove, are joined סיס sis and עגור agor, as birds that are likewise migratory, in these words of Ierem. VIII, 7. Both thor and sis and agor have kept the time of their coming. And since the turtledove has been dealt with, it follows that we treat of sis and agor. These words occur again in the song of King Hezekiah, Es. XXXVIII, 14. Like sis (he says) and agor I chirped, I moaned like a dove. But elsewhere there is no mention of them. And although in both places סוס is written in the text with Vau, yet in Jeremiah the Hebrews read סיס sis, with Iod. This reading I strongly approve, both so that סיס sis may differ from the word סוס sus, which means horse, and because סיס sis seems better to express the nature of the thing signified by this name ^{(1)}. This very point, since it is in question, must now be examined. Pagninus, Munster, Buxtorf, Schindler, Junius and Tremellius, the English, the Italians, etc., and most other modern interpreters consistently render סיס sis as crane. So, of course, the most learned of the Hebrews hold, Jarchi, Kimchi and Pomarius, following Jonathan in the Chaldee Paraphrase, which has כורכיא kurkeja for סיס sis. Further, that כורכיא kurkeja is the crane is clear both from the Talmud and from the Arab writers, who write كركي [kurkī] kurki. For כורכיא kurkeja you sometimes find כרוכיא krukeja, as in the tractate Kiddusim, ch. 2, fol. 44a. Very similar to this word is the word כרוכא kruka, which occurs in Jonathan at Levit. XI, 22. for חגב chagab, or cicada. It once also stood in the Jerusalem Paraphrase, from which it is cited by Elias in the Methurgeman. Hence arose an amusing error in Symmachus, who, taking the words כרוכא kruka and כרוכיא krukeja indiscriminately, made a cicada out of the crane in Jeremiah. Hence Jerome on Jeremiah: Symmachus translated it 'cicada', which in Hebrew is called סיס sis. And in the same place Theodoret: Τρυγὼν, καὶ τέττιξ, καὶ χελιδὼν, ἀγροῦ στρουθία, ἐφύλαξαν καιροὺς εἰσόδων αὐτῶν· [Trygōn, kai tettix, kai chelidōn, agrou strouthia, ephylaxan kairous eisodōn autōn] The turtledove, and the cicada, and the swallow, [II, 603] little birds of the field, have observed the time of their coming. After Chrysostom quoted these very words in the Homily On the Turtledove, as if from Jeremiah, he adds by way of commentary: Τρυγόνα λέγων τὴν πάνσεμνον ἐκκλησίαν, χελιδόνα τὸν φιλέρημον Ἰωάννην, τέττιγα τὸν εὔλαλον Παῦλον [Trygona legōn tēn pansemnon ekklēsian, chelidona ton philerēmon Iōannēn, tettiga ton eulalon Paulon]. Calling the venerable church the turtledove, the dweller in the desert, John, the swallow, and the eloquent Paul the cicada. This error arose from another error. For those who render סיס sis as crane are as mistaken as those who render it cicada: since סיס sis is neither the crane nor the cicada, but the swallow. This is proved first by the agreement of the older interpreters, which carries great weight with me when no compelling reason opposes it, and here none presents itself. As older interpreters I here name: 1. the Greek Elders, by whom סיס sis is rendered χελιδὼν [chelidōn] in both places; 2. Theodotion; 3. Jerome, who follow the same; 4. that very Symmachus for whom סיס sis in Jeremiah is the cicada. For by him Hezekiah's words כסוס עגור are rendered ὡς χελιδὼν ἐγκλεισθεῖσα [hōs chelidōn enkleistheisa], like a swallow shut in. 5. Add to these the Arabic translator, for whom סיס sis is سنونوه [sunūnūh] sununua, that is, swallow. In Abi Ubid, Century 1, Proverb 32, it is written سنونية [sunūniya] senunia, and the late Erpenius ὁ μακαρίτης [ho makaritēs] had rightly explained it as swallow, but only by conjecture. That it is the name of a bird, he says, is clear enough; but of what kind I do not know. I translated it swallow, because the Chaldee סנוניתא senunitha is usually so translated. Otherwise the swallow is called خطاف [khuṭṭāf] chottaph, etc. To meet these doubts of a man by far the most learned in Arabic letters, and once most deserving of my gratitude, I wish to explain the word more precisely. خطاف [khuṭṭāf] chottaph is the swallow in general, so called from the swiftness of its flight, like the Chaldee חטפיתא chatphitha. But of this there are several species, which the Arabs in Damir define thus: الخطاطيف انواع منها نوع يالف السواحل عند البحر يحفر بيتها هناك ويعشش هناك وهو صغير الجثة دون عصغور الجنة ولونه رمادي [al-khaṭāṭīf anwāʿ minhā nawʿ yaʾlaf al-sawāḥil ʿinda al-baḥr yaḥfir baytahā hunāka wa-yuʿashshish hunāka wa-huwa ṣaghīr al-jutha dūna ʿaṣghūr al-janna wa-lawnuhu ramādī] [col. 61] والناس يسمونه سنونوا بضم السين المهملة ونونين ومنها نوع لخضرته علي ظهرة بعض حمرة اصغر من الدرة تسميه اهل مصر الخضري لخضرته يغتات الغراش والذباب ونحو ذلك ومنها طويل الاجنحة رقيقها يالف الجبال وياكل النمل وهذا النوع يقال له السايم مغرب سامه ومنهم من يسمي هذا النوع السنونوا الوحدة سنونوة وهو كثير في المسجد الحرام بمكة يعشش في سقف المسجد في مقام ابراهيم وباب بني شيبة وبعض الناس [wa-al-nās yusammūnahu sunūnū bi-ḍamm al-sīn al-muhmala wa-nūnayn wa-minhā nawʿ li-khuḍratihi ʿalā ẓahrih baʿḍ ḥumra aṣghar min al-durra tusammīhi ahl Miṣr al-khuḍarī li-khuḍratihi yaghtāt al-gharāsh wa-al-dhubāb wa-naḥw dhālika wa-minhā ṭawīl al-ajniḥa raqīquhā yaʾlaf al-jibāl wa-yaʾkul al-naml wa-hādhā al-nawʿ yuqāl lahu al-sāyim mughrib sāmih wa-minhum man yusammī hādhā al-nawʿ al-sunūnū al-waḥda sunūnūa wa-huwa kathīr fī al-masjid al-ḥarām bi-Makka yuʿashshish fī saqf al-masjid fī maqām Ibrāhīm wa-bāb banī Shayba wa-baʿḍ al-nās] [II, 604] يزعم انه الطير الابابيل الذي عذب الله به اصحاب الغيل [yazʿum annahu al-ṭayr al-abābīl alladhī ʿadhdhaba Allāh bihi aṣḥāb al-ghīl] There are various species of swallows. One of them lives on the shores of the sea, and there digs out its home and nests. It is smaller in body than the bird of Paradise, and ash-grey in colour. It is called sununu, with Sin Semol given damma and two Nun. There is also a green species with some redness on the back, smaller than a parrot, which the Egyptians on account of its colour call chadra, that is, green. It feeds on butterflies, flies and other similar small creatures. There is also another species, with long and slender wings, a dweller in the mountains, which eats ants. These they call semaim, from the singular semama. But some also call them sununu. The singular of unity is sununua. Of this species there are many in the Charam temple of the city of Mecca, which nest in the roof of the temple, at the station of Abraham and at the gate of the sons of Seiba. Some assert that these are the birds called ababil, by which God punished the companions of the elephant: namely by throwing on their heads حجارة من سجيل [ḥijāra min sijjīl] stones of siggil. So they call stones baked and hardened in the fire of hell, inscribed with the names of those on whom they fell. Their leader Abraheth, king of the Abyssinians in the interior of Arabia Felix, in the very year in which Muhammad was born, had come riding a great elephant with large forces in order to destroy the temple of Mecca. The pseudo-prophet touches on this in passing in Azoara 115, entitled الغيل [al-ghīl] The Elephant. But these matters belong elsewhere. Here it suffices to have noted that it is clear from what has been adduced that سنونوة [sunūnūa] sununua properly denotes the sand martin [hirundo riparia] ^{(2)}, of which Pliny, book 10, ch. 33: The third kind of them is those which hollow out banks and so nest within. And book 30, ch. 4: Yet by far the most efficacious are the young of the bank (swallows). So they call those that nest in hollows of riverbanks. The riparia [bank swallow] is called in Greek δρεπανὶς [drepanis], from its sickle-shaped feet. So the Philosopher calls it, Hist. [col. 62] book 1, ch. 1. But they add that by the same name سنونوة [sunūnūa] sununua are also signified those swallows which nest in mountains and temples. These are the rustic or field swallows of Pliny, on which see Gesner, p. 565 ^{(3)}. Meanwhile it is certain that this name sometimes extends more widely and is used for any swallow. Thus the stone اليرقان [al-yaraqān] icterias, that is, by which jaundice sufferers are healed, is by another name called حجر السنونوة [ḥajar al-sunūnūa] the stone of the sununua, that is, of the swallow, because it is found in its nest. For the Arabs dye the swallow's young with saffron; and the father, suspecting that they suffer from jaundice, brings that stone from India into the nest and places it under the young. Damir describes it as small, streaked with red lines that verge on black. So too the author On the Wonders of Nature, where, as Damir notes, صنونو [ṣunūnū] sununu is wrongly read with Sad. And at Baruch. VI, 21. the Arabic translator rendered these Greek words, Ἐπὶ τὴν κεφαλὴν [II, 605] αὐτῶν ἐφίπτανται χελιδόνες [Epi tēn kephalēn autōn ephiptantai chelidones], thus: السنونو تلمسهم علي راسهم [al-sunūnū talmisuhum ʿalā raʾsihim] Assununu (or swallows) touch them upon their heads. Touch, that is, ἐφάπτονται [ephaptontai], as he read instead of ἐφίπτανται [ephiptantai], fly upon.
